source.title_on_document: Agency Configurations in Generative AI Ideation: How Textual and Visual Idea Concretizations Shape Idea Creativity and Ideator Effort

supplement.where: Online appendix at https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2024.0952 (PDF p. 2, article p. 1, ‘Supplemental Material’); not on file
supplement.holds: Per the main text, Online Appendix A contains exemplary interaction flows; B contains the concretization and LLM-judge prompts; C contains control-variable scale items; D contains descriptives and scale validation; E1 reports the bootstrap comparison of visual and textual concretizations at low idea maturity; E2 reports the separate Prolific sample using ChatGPT freely; E3 covers alternative operationalizations and modeling approaches (PDF pp. 8-12 and 14). The appendix is not included in the supplied PDF and has not been inspected. The main text gives no arm sizes, arm-level means or SDs, textual-versus-control coefficient or SE, separate novelty or usefulness results, numerical E1 bootstrap results, or S2 sample size, scoring method, analysis unit, or numerical statistics. It does not establish which of these missing quantities the appendix actually provides.

paper_design_summary: The main online experiment analyzed 276 U.S.-based Prolific participants who described and refined an idea for improving crowded-train travel; individual ideators were randomly assigned to an AI textual concretization, an AI visual concretization, or a no-AI imagination control. Creativity was scored on 428 post-initial idea refinements using automated novelty and usefulness measures, and effort was measured from keystrokes and time. The main text also reports a separate Prolific sample using ChatGPT freely and refers its comparison with the concretization arms to Online Appendix E2.

ai_tool.name_model: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (textual concretizations; also writes the DALL-E prompts) and DALL-E 3 (visual concretizations)
ai_tool.how_used: The platform sent the ideator's own initial idea description to the model, which returned a textual usage scenario or an image depicting the idea; the ideator then rewrote the idea description and could repeat the cycle, with a new concretization each time, until satisfied (Figure 3). The AI rendered the person's own idea rather than offering free chat.

task.description: ‘What improvements could be made to a crowded train to enhance the experience from boarding to alighting?’ (mirrors a public open-innovation challenge). Each participant provided one idea, described it in text, and refined it in one or more iterations.

outcomes.name: Idea creativity (mean of novelty and usefulness, z-standardized at the iteration level)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty: all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings, three-nearest-neighbor similarity among ideas at the same refinement iteration stage (the greater the distance to the most similar ideas, the higher the novelty; following Just et al. 2024). Usefulness: gpt-4o-2024-05-13 as judge of feasibility, elaboration, and inclusivity, each iteration scored three times and averaged; similar results with other models (e.g., Llama 70B: r = 0.73, p ≤ 0.01). Idea creativity = average of novelty and usefulness, standardized at the iteration level (endnote 4). Validation (endnote 3): 88 Prolific workers rated 158 ideas, each at least six times, ICC 0.6; correlation with the creativity score Pearson r = 0.27 (p ≤ 0.001), Spearman r = 0.24 (p ≤ 0.001), Kendall's tau = 0.16 (p ≤ 0.01). Robustness variants: Model 1b (controls), Model 1c (maturity interactions), bootstrap comparison of textual versus visual concretizations at low idea maturity (Online Appendix E1), alternative operationalizations (Online Appendix E3). Novelty and usefulness are not reported separately in the main text. OLS at the refinement level with clustered robust standard errors; the cluster level is not named. The 428 regression observations are refinements after the initial descriptions; initial ideas were scored separately for the baseline comparison and the novelty reference pool (PDF p. 10, Section 5; PDF p. 14, endnotes 4-5). Measure and validation details: PDF p. 9, Section 4.3.2, and PDF p. 14, endnotes 3-4.

contrasts.reported: Backward-difference contrast ‘Textual Concretization’ (textual vs visual): Model (1a) 0.29** (0.11); Model (1b, controls) 0.23* (0.10); Model (1c, maturity interactions) 0.20* (0.08). N = 428 refinements; clustered robust SEs; * p ≤ 0.05, ** p ≤ 0.01. Text: β = 0.29, p ≤ 0.01, ‘an improvement in creativity of 18%’. Endnote 6: 0.29 SDs; adjusted predictions 0.06 SDs below the mean (51st percentile) with visual vs 0.23 SDs above the mean (60th percentile) with textual, ‘approximately 18% ((60 − 51)/51)’. Textual Concretization × Idea Maturity 0.24** (0.09) in Model (1c). Bootstrap robustness analysis (Online Appendix E1, summarized in Section 5): for ideas more than one SD below mean maturity, visual concretizations significantly outperformed textual concretizations in creativity without increasing effort; above this threshold, textual concretizations produced more creative ideas with greater effort. This is a reversal of the main-effect direction for very immature ideas; no numerical bootstrap effect, SE, or p-value is printed in the main text.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 10 (article p. 9), Table 2 and Section 5; PDF p. 14 (article p. 13), endnote 6; PDF p. 11 (article p. 10), Figure 4 and Section 5, first robustness check; PDF p. 12 (article p. 11), Section 6, first paragraph

contrasts.reported: Backward-difference contrast ‘Visual Concretization’ (visual vs control): Model (1a) 0.13 (0.10); Model (1b, controls) 0.17† (0.10), † p ≤ 0.10; Model (1c) 0.14 (0.10). N = 428 refinements; outcome in SD units. Text: ‘a slight improvement for visual concretizations relative to the control group (β = 0.17, p ≤ 0.1)’. Visual Concretization × Idea Maturity 0.04 (0.13). eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Individual ideators were randomly assigned to experimental groups (PDF p. 13, article p. 12, Section 6.3) in a three-cell, between-subjects online experiment with textual AI, visual AI, and no-AI conditions (PDF p. 8, article p. 7, Section 4.1). The analysis covers 276 people and their 428 idea refinements: Section 4.2 reports both counts, Table 2 analyzes N = 428, and endnote 5 identifies N as refinements submitted across all ideators (PDF pp. 9-10 and 14). The number randomized and arm sizes are not stated; 276 is recorded as analyzed. Creativity is scored on the produced refinements using embedding-based novelty and GPT-4o-judged usefulness (PDF p. 9, Section 4.3.2; PDF p. 14, endnotes 3-4), after the AI concretization was shown (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1). S2 is a separate-sample comparison with no random assignment reported; its missing scoring method, analysis unit, sample size, and statistics do not change S1 eligibility.

one_line_finding: Among 276 analyzed Prolific ideators (428 refinements), textual AI concretizations raised automated idea creativity by 0.29 SD over visual AI concretizations (Model 1a, SE 0.11) and by a reported, statistically significant 30% over the no-AI control (no coefficient printed), while visual versus control was 0.13 SD (SE 0.10, not significant) (PDF p. 9, article p. 8, Section 4.2 for the sample; PDF p. 10, article p. 9, Table 2 and Section 5).
open_questions: S1 arm sizes at assignment and analysis, and any exclusions, are not stated in the main text; Online Appendix D is cited for descriptives and may clarify them. The total analyzed count of 276 people is supported.

The number assigned before any exclusions remains unstated: Section 4.2 calls the 276 people recruited, while Table 2 and endnote 5 support 276 analyzed people. The source does not provide an enrollment or attrition flow.

Textual versus control is described as a statistically significant 30% increase, but no coefficient, SE, p-value, or basis for the percentage is printed. Author clarification or the underlying model output is needed; no effect was calculated.
The standard errors are described as clustered robust, but the cluster identifier is not explicitly named (PDF p. 10, Section 5). This affects suitability for pooling, not core screening eligibility.
Creativity is standardized at the iteration level; the main text reports no participant-level SD. Participant-linked data would permit later aggregation for effect extraction.
Separate novelty and usefulness results are not reported in the main text; Online Appendix E3 covers alternative operationalizations, but its contents have not been inspected.

S2: Online Appendix E2 is needed to establish sample size, recruitment and comparison procedures, scoring method, analysis unit, and numerical results. The main text supports only the direction of the creativity comparison and identifies a separate Prolific sample using ChatGPT freely.
notes: Contrasts use backward-difference coding: ‘Textual Concretization’ = textual vs visual; ‘Visual Concretization’ = visual vs control (PDF p. 9, article p. 8, Section 4.3.1). The control arm received imagination instructions, not an alternative aid, so it is coded as no AI (ai_vs_bau). Outcomes not listed because they answer none of the three questions: ideator effort (log of the mean of scaled keystrokes and time spent; Table 2 Model 2a: visual vs control −0.26*** (0.07), textual vs visual 0.24** (0.08); visual reduced effort 24% relative to control, textual required 30% more than visual, no textual-vs-control difference) and idea maturity (text-scored specificity and actionability, Yeomans 2021), which is a moderator. The human-rater validation in endnote 3 (88 raters, 158 ideas) checks the measure and is not a separate experiment. AI role coded refinement: the models rendered the participant's own idea as a usage-scenario text or an image, and the participant rewrote the idea. Locators give the PDF page with the article page in parentheses; PDF page 1 is the INFORMS cover sheet. Search-record leads: ‘N=276 with no unit stated’ is 276 people; ‘without stated random assignment’ is wrong, since random assignment is stated on PDF p. 13 (article p. 12). The retrieval log lists a 2025 EMAC extended abstract by the same five authors that reports no data; the document names no other paper that uses these participants. Finalization: the full supplied markdown, including endnotes, references, and the correction notice, was read. Relevant PDF text and Table 2 were checked, and Figure 4 was inspected. The 428 observations are post-initial refinements (Section 5 and endnotes 4-5), so that former open question is settled. The textual-versus-visual direction code describes the positive main effect; the opposite direction for very immature ideas is documented in that contrast’s robustness results. S2 measure and unit are null because neither is stated; scored_on_output remains true because the source explicitly compares the creativity of the produced ideas. The reconciliation object is preserved as the historical record; final.challenge_resolution records the corrections that supersede its earlier conclusions about S2 measurement and textual-versus-control statistics.

open_items.item: Arm sizes at assignment and analysis, and any exclusions, are unstated. Appendix D is the cited source for descriptives and should be checked; these missing arm-level details do not affect the confirmed total of 276 analyzed people.

Whether 276 also equals the number randomized, and whether any people were excluded before analysis, remains unknown. Author confirmation of the enrollment and attrition flow would settle this; Section 4.2, Table 2, and endnote 5 already support 276 analyzed people for criterion 2.

The former question about inclusion of initial descriptions in N = 428 is settled: Section 5 analyzes effects beyond the initially submitted ideas and endnote 5 defines N as idea refinements; endnote 4 distinguishes initial ideas from first refinements (PDF pp. 10 and 14). The analyzed outcomes follow the AI input.

The textual-versus-control coefficient, SE, p-value, and basis of the reported 30% increase remain unstated. Authors could provide the contrast output and explain the percentage; these affect effect extraction rather than any eligibility criterion.

The cluster identifier for the reported clustered robust SEs is not explicitly named. Authors could confirm the clustering specification; this determines pooling suitability, not random assignment, analyzed sample size, or output scoring.

No participant-level SD is reported for creativity, which was standardized at the iteration level. Participant-linked posted data would permit aggregation and a participant-level SD for later extraction; no eligibility criterion depends on this standardizer.

Separate novelty and usefulness estimates are absent from the main text. Appendix E3 is cited for alternative operationalizations and should be checked for these outcomes; the documented composite creativity score already meets criterion 3.

S2 sample size, recruitment and comparison procedures, scoring method, analysis unit, and numerical statistics need Online Appendix E2. These are gaps in coding the separate-sample context comparison; S1 independently meets all three criteria, so paper eligibility is unaffected.
